name: Airfrog
firmware_note: Single official Rust firmware (embassy + esp-hal) you build and flash yourself with cargo/espflash; no assembled/pre-flashed option exists. Provides web, REST and binary APIs plus probe-rs integration; custom apps can be built against the same libraries.
price_note: No assembled unit is sold by anyone found in this research. Per the project's own FAQ, the BOM (ESP32-C3-MINI-1-N4 module ~$3, plus an AP2112K-3.3 LDO and a handful of passives per the rev-b BOM) comes to 'well under $5 per unit even in very low quantities.' Add PCB fab (a few dollars for a small panel from a standard fab house) and your own soldering time/equipment; JLCPCB's standard SMT service will not place the ESP32 module, only their pricier 'advanced assembly' tier will.
skill_note: Hand-soldering 0402 passives and a QFN-style ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module onto a coin-sized 2-layer board, wiring SWD to a target, and building Rust firmware with cargo are all required; the resulting web UI itself is simple to use once it's running.
build_note: No kit is sold. You fabricate the 2-layer PCB yourself from the provided Gerbers (rev-b BOM: ESP32-C3-MINI-1-N4, AP2112K-3.3, 8 passives), hand-solder it, then build and flash the Rust firmware yourself via `cargo run --release -p airfrog`.
summary: Airfrog is an open-source, coin-sized (16x28mm) PCB built around a $3 ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module that bit-bangs the SWD protocol to an ARM Cortex-M target and exposes its RAM, flash and peripherals over Wi-Fi via a web UI, a REST API, and a low-overhead binary API, plus probe-rs integration. It's designed to stay wired to one target permanently - the way a network card lives inside a PC - rather than being carried between different boards like a USB debug probe.
honest_take: This is a wireless SWD bridge for one target, not a general-purpose debug probe you carry between boards - it has no JTAG, only SWD, and has only been tested by the author against STM32F1/F4 and the RP2040/Pico. It's a single-developer project that saw two and a half months of rapid commits (July-September 2025) and then went completely silent - no commits and no replies to any of its 22 open feature-request issues for a full year as of this check. The core idea (debug + telemetry over Wi-Fi without a wired connection) is genuinely useful and not something Tigard or Glasgow Interface Explorer do, but those wired, multi-protocol probes (JTAG/SWD/UART/SPI/I2C) are instantly usable, ship assembled, and don't require permanently wiring hardware to a target - if you just want a working debug probe today, they're the safer choice. The ESP32-C3 silicon is the same family widely used for Wi-Fi deauth/monitor-mode tools elsewhere, but Airfrog's firmware doesn't implement any of that - its Wi-Fi radio exists purely as the SWD backhaul.
best_for: Adding a permanent wireless telemetry/debug channel to a target ARM device you control
Reprogramming or monitoring an embedded device over Wi-Fi without ongoing physical access
Learning embedded Rust and SWD protocol internals from a small, readable codebase
not_for: General-purpose portable debugging across many different target boards - it's meant to stay wired to one
JTAG targets - SWD only
Anyone who wants a ready-to-use assembled probe rather than a soldering-plus-Rust-toolchain project

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Single-core RISC-V @160MHz, 400KB SRAM, 4MB integrated flash (N4 variant). Module includes 2.4GHz 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5 LE, though only Wi-Fi is used by the firmware.

radios.note: 2.4GHz 802.11 b/g/n; DHCP client plus a captive AP mode for first-time setup. Used purely as the SWD-over-network backhaul, not for any Wi-Fi security functions.

hardware.battery_note: No battery. Powered by 5V from a host/USB source via the 5-pin target header or the UART programming header; onboard AP2112K-3.3 LDO regulates to 3.3V.
hardware.pmic: AP2112K-3.3 (LDO regulator, not a full PMIC)
hardware.storage: 4MB flash integrated in the ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module (firmware/config only, not used to store target data)
hardware.gpio: 5-pin target connector (5V power, SWDIO, SWCLK, GND, 1 reserved/unused pin); separate 6-pin UART programming header exposes TX/RX/GND/VCC/EN/IO9-BOOT
notable_physical: Separate self-programming header so one Airfrog can flash another

uart.note: Dedicated 6-pin UART header used for flashing/programming and log output at selectable levels (error through trace).

jtag_swd.note: SWD only, no JTAG. Bit-banged on ESP32-C3 GPIOs at 500KHz/1MHz/2MHz/4MHz (Turbo, default); tested against STM32F1, STM32F4 and RP2040/Pico. Integrates with probe-rs via a fork.

spi_flash_dump.note: Reads/writes/erases target flash via the SWD debug port (not a native SPI interface) using the REST/binary API or probe-rs.

i2c.note: No I2C bridge - the 5-pin target connector carries only power, ground and the two SWD lines.

logic_analyzer.note: Not a logic analyzer; purely an SWD debug/programming bridge.

glitching.note: No fault-injection capability of any kind.

sd_logging.note: No SD card slot; onboard flash is used only for the device's own firmware/config.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: The ESP32-C3 silicon supports Wi-Fi monitor mode in other projects, but Airfrog's firmware only uses the radio as a plain Wi-Fi client/AP for its own web and API traffic - no packet capture or injection is implemented.

wifi_deauth_24.note: Not implemented. Worth stating explicitly since the ESP32-C3 is the same chip family used for deauth tools elsewhere - Airfrog's firmware doesn't do this.

ble_scan.note: The ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module's BLE radio is present in silicon but is not initialized or used by Airfrog's firmware at all.

web_ui.note: Built-in web interface for memory/RAM/flash/peripheral access, served from the ESP32 itself.

scriptable.note: REST API (JSON/HTTP) and a low-overhead binary TCP API for scripting; custom firmware apps can be built in Rust against the provided libraries.

standalone_untethered.note: Once flashed with Wi-Fi credentials it runs standalone, reachable over the network with no host PC required for ongoing operation.

legal.notes: Not a radio transmitter beyond the pre-certified ESP32-C3 Wi-Fi module, and not designed to attack devices you don't control. Owning and building it is uncontroversial in essentially all jurisdictions; using SWD access to bypass another party's device protections without authorization can implicate computer-misuse law the same as any other debug probe. This is general information, not legal advice - check your local law.

name: Curious Bolt
firmware_note: Single vendor firmware (RP2040 C, TinyUSB + Raspberry Pi Pico SDK) ships pre-flashed. Implements the SUMP logic-analyzer protocol, a PIO/DMA-driven crowbar glitcher, an ADC-based power scope, and a 4-channel programmable I/O pattern generator, all controlled over USB-serial.
price_note: Sold as the 'Curious Bolt limited Edition' bundle through Curious Supplies' production partner Allnet (shop.allnetchina.cn), SKU CD-CBOLTKIT, confirmed live in the storefront's own product JSON as of the check date. Price covers the whole kit - the Bolt board, an STM32F103 target board with the 4 ECSC23 hardware challenges, a separate STM32 SWD programmer, Dupont cables and logic-analyzer probes - not the Bolt alone.
skill_note: Voltage glitching and differential power analysis both require understanding the attack you're attempting and iterating with the bundled Python library; it was built for a cybersecurity-competition (ECSC 2023) audience, not total beginners, though the included challenges give a structured on-ramp.
build_note: Ships as a populated, ready-to-use board; no soldering. You do need to install Python + pyserial and, for the logic analyzer, PulseView/sigrok.
summary: The Curious Bolt is a Raspberry Pi RP2040-based hardware-hacking multitool combining three functions on one small board: a PIO-driven crowbar voltage glitcher with roughly 8.3ns timing resolution, an 8-channel logic analyzer speaking the SUMP protocol (works directly in PulseView/sigrok), and a 10-bit ADC used as a differential power-analysis scope. It originated as the hardware for the 2023 European Cyber Security Challenge (ECSC23) in Oslo and is now sold as a 'limited edition' kit bundled with the STM32F103 target board and four challenges used in that competition.
honest_take: The RP2040 is doing essentially all the real-time work here - its PIO state machines generate the glitch pulses and clock the logic-analyzer/ADC sampling - so this is fundamentally a well-executed RP2040 project, not custom silicon; the actual engineering is in the PIO programs and the MS9280 parallel ADC front end. It sits in the same functional niche as the well-established ChipWhisperer-Nano and ChipWhisperer-Lite (glitcher plus power-analysis capture on one board), which have a far bigger user base and published courses behind them; Bolt's differential-power-scope mode is explicitly marked 'documentation in progress' by the vendor, making it the least mature of its three advertised functions. The firmware repo has had no commits since February 2024 and carries an open issue literally titled 'Firmware build instructions' because there aren't any in the repo - fine if you only ever run it as shipped, a real obstacle if you want to modify the firmware yourself. It is also not a JTAG/SWD debug probe or a UART bridge, despite being marketed as a general 'security multitool' - those are separate categories of tool it doesn't touch.
best_for: Learning voltage glitching and logic analysis together on one board with a guided target (the ECSC23 challenges)
Cheap 8-channel logic analysis via existing PulseView/sigrok tooling
A structured intro to fault injection for students or CTF-style training
not_for: Production or professional power-analysis work - the scope function is the least documented of the three and has far less tooling than ChipWhisperer
Anyone wanting to build or modify the firmware themselves - no build instructions exist in the repo as of this check
JTAG/SWD debugging or general UART bridging - it does neither

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual-core Cortex-M0+ @133MHz (Raspberry Pi Pico SDK-based firmware). PIO blocks and DMA channels do the real-time glitch triggering, logic-analyzer sampling and GPIO pattern generation; confirmed from firmware/bolt/CMakeLists.txt (pico_sdk_import.cmake) and the PIO assembly in glitch.c/adc.c/output.c.
connectivity: USB (2x CDC-ACM serial interfaces: control protocol + SUMP logic-analyzer stream)
hardware.gpio: 8 logic-analyzer input channels, 1 glitcher 'sig' output pin, 4 programmable I/O output channels (100MHz PIO-clocked pattern generator), 1 ADC input for the power scope
notable_physical: MS9280 10-bit parallel ADC (Hangzhou Ruimeng Tech, ~35MSPS per JLCPCB's listing) for the power-scope function
Onboard switching stage for the crowbar glitch output

glitching.note: Crowbar-style voltage glitcher (pulls the target rail to ground), driven by an RP2040 PIO program in ~8.3ns steps (one 120MHz clock cycle). Triggerable manually, in a loop, or off an external signal edge with a programmable delay.

logic_analyzer.note: 8 channels, SUMP-protocol compatible, works directly with sigrok/PulseView over USB-serial. Vendor's landing page states 100k sample memory points; this research confirmed the SUMP/PIO/DMA implementation in firmware source but not that exact depth figure, so treat the specific number as vendor-claimed.

uart.note: No general-purpose UART bridge to a target - the two USB-CDC interfaces carry only Bolt's own control protocol and the SUMP logic-analyzer stream.

jtag_swd.note: Not a debug probe - no JTAG or SWD support despite being marketed as a 'security multitool.'

i2c.note: No dedicated I2C master/bridge function; the logic analyzer can passively observe I2C traffic on its input channels but cannot drive the bus.

spi_flash_dump.note: No SPI flash programming/dump mode documented.

sd_logging.note: No SD card; captures are streamed live to a host PC over USB.

scriptable.note: Python library (lib/scope.py, pyserial-based) exposes glitcher, ADC and I/O control for scripting.

web_ui.note: No web interface - control is via the Python library or PulseView over USB-serial.

standalone_untethered.note: Requires a host PC (Python script or PulseView) for every function; no standalone/field mode.

legal.notes: A voltage glitcher, logic analyzer and power-analysis scope for hardware you own or are authorized to test; no radio, no restricted crypto. Using it to defeat protections on a device you don't own or aren't authorized to test can implicate computer-misuse or anti-circumvention law depending on jurisdiction. This is general information, not legal advice - check your local law.

name: Steppenprobe
firmware_note: No user-flashable firmware. The board is an FTDI FT2232H USB-to-MPSSE/UART bridge chip configured entirely by host-side software (OpenOCD, standard FTDI drivers) - there is nothing on the board itself to build or flash.
price_note: No vendor sells this assembled or as a kit. Estimated from the project's own JLCPCB-format BOM: the dominant cost is the FT2232HL USB UART/FIFO chip (~$5.30 in single quantities per DigiKey), plus a USB-C receptacle, 12MHz crystal, ESD-protection and logic-buffer ICs, and roughly 50 passives (an estimated $5-8 total at low volume), plus a small 2-layer PCB fab run (a few dollars per board for 5-10pcs from a standard fab house). Excludes your own assembly time/equipment - hand-soldering the FT2232HL's 0.5mm-pitch LQFP-64 package is nontrivial.
skill_note: You fab your own PCB from the provided Gerbers and hand-solder an LQFP-64 0.5mm-pitch FTDI chip plus SOT-23/SC-70 logic ICs yourself (or pay a fab house for assembly), then configure OpenOCD by hand. No kit, no guided build, no assembled option from anyone.
build_note: KiCad source, schematic PDF, Gerbers/Excellon, and JLCPCB-format BOM/CPL files are published (v1.0 release, 2020), but no one - including the original author - appears to sell it assembled. You order the PCB and parts yourself and solder it.
summary: Steppenprobe is a one-person, open-hardware (KiCad) debug probe built around an FTDI FT2232H dual-channel USB bridge: channel A does JTAG or SWD (OpenOCD-compatible, no jumpers needed), channel B does UART or SWO trace, and both run simultaneously over a single USB-C cable to a 14-pin STDC14 Cortex debug connector (backward compatible with the standard 10-pin ARM connector). It also exposes 4 general-purpose GPIO controllable from OpenOCD.
honest_take: Steppenprobe uses the exact same core chip as Tigard - the FT2232H - and Tigard's own README describes itself as 'an FTDI FT2232H-based multi-protocol tool for hardware hacking.' The difference is what's built around that chip: Tigard also does SPI, I2C, AVR ISP and iCE40 programming and ships assembled and ready to use, while Steppenprobe is JTAG/SWD/UART/SWO only and you have to fab and hand-solder the board yourself from Gerbers - no one sells it assembled. If you don't specifically need simultaneous JTAG/SWD plus UART/SWO on one USB-C cable, or don't want to hand-solder an LQFP-64 0.5mm-pitch part, Tigard or the Glasgow Interface Explorer get you a working, more capable probe faster. The project itself is functionally frozen: the last real code change was in 2021/2022, and a 2024 commit only re-saved the same files for KiCad 8 compatibility with no functional change. It has 0 open issues, which reads less as 'bug-free' and more as 'nobody is actively filing against it anymore' - though 11 forks suggest some people did build on it.
best_for: Simultaneous JTAG/SWD debugging and UART/SWO trace capture on one USB-C connection
Learning OpenOCD/FTDI MPSSE internals by building your own probe from a fully open KiCad design
A minimal, single-purpose JTAG/SWD+UART probe if you're already comfortable fabricating and hand-soldering your own boards
not_for: Anyone who wants to buy a working probe rather than build one - no assembled units exist
SPI or I2C work - Tigard and Glasgow Interface Explorer cover far more protocols on the same class of hardware
Beginners - hand-soldering an LQFP-64 0.5mm-pitch FTDI chip is not a first-solder-project task

hardware.mcu_primary_note: No MCU - the board is built around an FTDI FT2232HL, a fixed-function dual-channel USB-to-MPSSE/UART bridge IC, not a programmable microcontroller.
connectivity: 2.54mm pin header breakout for custom pinouts
hardware.gpio: 4 GPIO (GPIO_A-D), high-impedance by default, settable/readable via OpenOCD's ftdi_set_signal/ftdi_get_signal commands
notable_physical: FT2232HL LQFP-64 as the sole active IC (plus small logic buffers)
Physical switch selecting UART RX vs SWO on channel B

uart.note: FT2232H channel B, up to 12Mbps (4Mbps reliably on modern Linux without custom divisors), switchable with SWO via a physical switch.

jtag_swd.note: FT2232H channel A in MPSSE mode; JTAG or SWD selected in software via OpenOCD ('transport select swd'), no jumpers. OpenOCD-compatible from v0.11.0.

logic_analyzer.note: No logic-analyzer mode or sigrok/PulseView support documented - notable since comparable FT2232H-based probes (Tigard) and other tracked debug tools (Bus Pirate 5, Glasgow Interface Explorer) commonly add this.

i2c.note: Not exposed - only JTAG/SWD and UART/SWO are wired up on this design, unlike Tigard which uses the same chip family for I2C too.

spi_flash_dump.note: No dedicated SPI/flash-programming mode documented in the OpenOCD interface config; only JTAG/SWD target-flash programming through a debug core, same as any debug probe.

glitching.note: Pure debug/trace probe - no fault-injection capability.

scriptable.note: No onboard scripting; it is a passive USB-to-MPSSE/UART bridge entirely driven by host-side OpenOCD.

standalone_untethered.note: Requires a host PC running OpenOCD (or a serial terminal) at all times; cannot operate independently.

web_ui.note: No network interface or web UI of any kind - USB only.

sd_logging.note: No storage on the board; all capture happens on the connected host.

legal.notes: A standard JTAG/SWD/UART debug adapter for hardware you own or are authorized to test; no radio, nothing export-controlled. Using it against a device's security/debug-lockout protections without authorization can raise the same computer-misuse concerns as any other debug probe. This is general information, not legal advice - check your local law.

name: Cypherock EMFI Board
firmware_note: STM32CubeIDE project (STM32 HAL) implementing a PID voltage-control loop over PWM plus a USB-CDC serial command protocol for arming/triggering shots and reading back voltage. You build and flash it yourself via STM32CubeIDE; there is no separate firmware distribution or pre-flashed option.
price_note: No vendor sells this assembled; Cypherock (a hardware-wallet company) published it as an open research artifact, not a product. Rough estimate from the Altium BOM (EMFI_BOM.xlsx) in the repo: STM32L412C8T6 MCU (~$3), IXGA30N120B3 1200V IGBT (~$1-1.50 in low qty per Newark), TPS61040 boost converter (~$1.50), a Coilcraft SCS-200LD transformer (no public unit price found, budgeted ~$8-10), roughly 24 1000V-rated ceramic capacitors forming the voltage-multiplier/reservoir bank, 3 SMA connectors, 2 USB-C receptacles, the 3D-printed protective enclosure (STEP files provided), and PCB fab. Likely range is $50-80 in low-volume parts; $65 used as a point estimate. Excludes the separate hand-wound EM probe and your build time/equipment.
skill_note: This is a roughly 1kV pulsed high-voltage device you build and hand-tune yourself, aimed at bypassing MCU read-out protection - it assumes you already understand fault-injection methodology, EMFI probe positioning, and high-voltage safety. A field report (see honest_take) describes the switching transistor, and on a repeat attempt the STM32 itself, being destroyed during first bring-up on a unit built exactly as documented.
build_note: No kit or assembled unit exists. You fab the Altium-designed PCB, source and solder the BOM (including a 1200V IGBT and 1000V-rated capacitors), 3D-print the provided enclosure, hand-wind your own EM injection probe from a power inductor and SMA connector, and build/flash the STM32CubeIDE firmware project yourself.
summary: The Cypherock EMFI Board is an open-hardware electromagnetic fault-injection tool: a USB-powered, STM32L412-controlled boost converter and a 1200V IGBT (IXGA30N120B3) drive a step-up transformer and diode voltage multiplier into a bank of 1000V-rated capacitors, then discharge through a hand-built EM probe coil to inject a fast electromagnetic pulse timed against a target chip. Cypherock, a hardware crypto-wallet maker, designed and published it to research fault-injection and read-out-protection-bypass attacks against microcontroller families (STM32, ATSAMD, ATmega, ESP32) and a crypto-authentication IC used in wallets like their own, and shipped 8 matching DUT target boards for exactly that testing.
honest_take: This sits in ChipSHOUTER territory - a purpose-built EMFI pulse generator - not ChipSHOUTER-PicoEMP territory; the PicoEMP is a much simpler, lower-voltage board, while this one runs a closed-loop PID voltage regulator up to roughly 1kV through a real IGBT switching stage, which is meaningfully more dangerous and more capable to build and operate. The single most important thing to know before attempting this: an open GitHub issue (filed August 2025, still unanswered as of this research) reports that the IGBT (Q1) self-excites and destroys itself on first power-up as designed, because it's switched directly by a logic-level MOSFET (Q3) instead of a proper isolated gate driver - and that repeated rebuild attempts destroyed further parts, including the STM32 MCU. Cypherock has not commented, and the repo has had zero commits since January 2024, so treat this as an unmaintained, reportedly broken-as-published design rather than a working product - budget for spare IGBTs and STM32s, or look at the actively-maintained ChipSHOUTER if you need something that works out of the box. The repo also ships 8 DUT boards (STM32F205RET6, STM32F427VIT6TR, STM32L496RGT6, STM32H753VIT6, ESP32-D0WD-V3, ATSAMD51J20A-AU, ATMEGA328P-AU, and an ATECC secure-element board), not the 7 MCU families the README's prose lists - the text and the actual hardware folder disagree by one.
best_for: Researchers who already have EMFI experience and want an open reference design to build and modify rather than buy a commercial unit
Studying read-out-protection bypass and control-flow fault attacks against the specific MCU/secure-element families it ships DUT boards for
not_for: Anyone without prior high-voltage or fault-injection experience - see the unresolved Q1 self-destruction report
Anyone who wants a working device without a rebuild-and-debug cycle - build it exactly as documented and there's a credible, unaddressed report it destroys its own IGBT and possibly the MCU
A first EMFI project - the already-tracked ChipSHOUTER-PicoEMP is a simpler, lower-voltage starting point

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Arm Cortex-M4, 32-bit, 80MHz (per the BOM's own part description). Runs the PID voltage-regulation loop and the USB-CDC serial control protocol; confirmed from firmware/Core/Startup/startup_stm32l412c8tx.s and the EMFI_BOM.xlsx part description.
connectivity: 2x SMA connectors for the EM probe (polarity-reversible)
1x SMA/pin header for external trigger input
hardware.gpio: External trigger input pin for hardware-timed shots (in addition to serial 'software shoot' commands); 3 onboard status LEDs
hardware.case: 3D-printed two-part enclosure (STEP files provided), described by the vendor as protection against exposure to the internal high-voltage circuitry
notable_physical: Coilcraft SCS-200LD transformer (a 1:200 current-sense transformer repurposed here as a step-up transformer) feeding a x4 diode voltage multiplier
Bank of 1000V-rated ceramic capacitors as the pulse reservoir
Separate hand-built EM probe (user-sourced power inductor + SMA connector, not included)

glitching.note: Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI), not voltage-rail crowbar glitching: a closed-loop PID-controlled boost stage charges a capacitor bank built from 1000V-rated components, discharged through an IGBT into a hand-wound EM probe coil, timed via a serial 'software shoot' command or an external hardware trigger pin. An open, unresolved GitHub issue reports the IGBT driver circuit self-destructs on first power-up as designed - see honest_take.

uart.note: USB-CDC serial at 9600 baud for arming, triggering, voltage-setpoint and PID-tuning commands (Scripts/Cypherock/cypherock.py); not a UART bridge to a third-party target.

jtag_swd.note: No onboard debug probe. The README describes pairing this board with a separate JTAG/SWD probe (e.g. for crash detection/recovery on the target) rather than including one.

spi_flash_dump.note: No SPI flash interface - this board only delivers the EM pulse, it doesn't read target memory itself.

logic_analyzer.note: No logic-analyzer or waveform-capture function onboard.

scriptable.note: Python control script (Scripts/Cypherock/cypherock.py) over serial: on/off, PWM settings, voltage setpoint, software-triggered shoot, PID tuning.

web_ui.note: No network interface or web UI - USB-serial control only.

standalone_untethered.note: Requires a host PC running the Python control script (or a terminal sending raw serial commands) for every operation; no standalone field mode.

sd_logging.note: No onboard storage; all control and readback happens live over the USB-serial link.

legal.notes: Not a radio transmitter and not export-controlled crypto; owning/building a research EMFI tool is uncontroversial in most jurisdictions, similar to the already-tracked ChipSHOUTER. Using it to defeat the read-out protection of a device you don't own or lack authorization to test can implicate computer-misuse or anti-circumvention law depending on jurisdiction. It also involves genuinely dangerous voltages (~1kV) - a safety concern independent of any legal one. This is general information, not legal advice - check your local law.

name: ChipWhisperer-Pro (CW1200)
firmware_note: Same open-source ChipWhisperer Python API and capture firmware as the rest of the line; the Pro exposes extra FPGA-based trigger modules (analog SAD, SPI decode, UART decode) through the same interface.
price_note: No longer sold. NewAE's own documentation flags it discontinued and points buyers to the Husky instead. Could not find an archived list price - web.archive.org was unreachable from this research environment, and historical distributor listings for the NAE-CW1200-KIT SKU (TrustedParts, digchip) returned no readable price.
skill_note: Same underlying discipline as the Lite/Nano/Husky - differential power analysis and fault injection - plus a more complex trigger/streaming setup that assumes you already know why you want SAD triggering or SPI/UART-pattern triggers.
build_note: Sold assembled as the 'ChipWhisperer-Pro Complete Level 3 Starter Kit' with a CW308 target platform, CW308T-XMEGA and CW308T-STM32F3 target boards, H-field and differential probes, a probe power supply, a 20dB LNA and analogue filters.
summary: The former top tier of NewAE's ChipWhisperer capture-hardware line: a 10-bit, 105 MS/s ADC with a 98,119-sample buffer, streaming capture up to 10 MS/s, a 5-200 MHz synchronous clock generator, four trigger module types (basic edge/level, analog SAD, SPI decode and UART decode), and both crowbar voltage glitching and clock glitching. It used the same FPGA-based architecture and 20-pin target connector as the ChipWhisperer-Lite, just with far more FPGA resources behind it, plus an onboard touchscreen the Lite and Husky don't have.
honest_take: NewAE's own current documentation states plainly that the CW1200 is discontinued and tells buyers to get a ChipWhisperer-Husky instead - and the Husky beats it outright on paper (12-bit/200 MS/s vs 10-bit/105 MS/s, a bigger buffer, and a newer VCO-based clock-glitch design), presumably at a fraction of the Pro's original price. This is a genuinely different product from the ChipWhisperer-Nano despite the naming similarity people sometimes assume: the Nano was always the ~$50 fixed-function education board with an 8-bit/20 MS/s ADC and no clock glitching at all, while the Pro was NewAE's flagship lab instrument aimed at labs already committed to the platform - different market tier, different silicon, not a rebrand or a variant of the same board. If you already own one, it is still a genuinely capable 10-bit/105 MS/s instrument with trigger modules the Lite lacks (SAD, SPI/UART decode) - it just is not the thing to go buy today, and a used unit carries the usual risk of an FPGA design nobody at NewAE is actively patching anymore.

Labs that specifically need SPI/UART-pattern or SAD triggering and can find one used
Understanding the historical ChipWhisperer product line before evaluating a Husky
not_for: New purchases - buy a ChipWhisperer-Husky instead
Anyone comparing it to the ChipWhisperer-Nano - wrong tier entirely, not a substitute
Budget-conscious hobbyists - even used, this was priced as lab equipment

name: CW305 Artix FPGA Target Board
firmware_note: The onboard SAM3U microcontroller (USB/board control, not the security target) runs NewAE's stock firmware from a separate repo to the main chipwhisperer package. The Artix-7 FPGA itself takes a user-supplied bitstream (e.g. a hardware AES/ECC core) - that bitstream, not this firmware, is what a side-channel or fault-injection attack actually targets.
price_note: NewAE's own storefront no longer carries it - the product-page URL 404s and the old store.newae.com subdomain no longer resolves at all (NXDOMAIN). Distributor Electromaker still lists both FPGA variants (SKUs NAE-CW305-04-7A35-0.10-X and -7A100-0.10-X) as 'In Stock' at $1,462.50, but both SKUs show the identical figure, which reads like a stale or templated price rather than confirmed current per-variant pricing.
skill_note: You are expected to bring or write your own FPGA bitstream (Verilog/VHDL crypto core) and a Vivado project - this is a target for people already doing FPGA-based side-channel or fault-injection research, not a beginner board.
build_note: Ships assembled. Available soldered or in a socketed-FPGA variant (swap FPGAs without resoldering) per the distributor SKU listings.
summary: A standalone Artix-7 FPGA target board built specifically to be attacked: it carries a socketable or soldered XC7A35T or XC7A100T FPGA, diode-protected power rails built for fault injection, dedicated shunt-resistor measurement points, and the standard 20-pin ChipWhisperer connector, so a CW1200/Lite/Husky can run power analysis or voltage-glitching experiments against whatever crypto core you load into the FPGA. NewAE ships example AES cores and Vivado projects to get started. It is the target, not the attack tool - by itself it does nothing.
honest_take: This is not an attack tool at all - it is the victim board, and it only does anything once paired with a real ChipWhisperer capture unit (Lite, Husky, or the now-discontinued Pro) and your own FPGA bitstream. NewAE appears to have quietly walked away from selling it directly: the product page 404s and their old storefront domain is dead, even though the ChipWhisperer documentation still lists it as a supported target. Distributor stock exists (around $1,460, which is suspiciously identical across both FPGA sizes and probably stale), but there's no confirmed live channel to buy new from NewAE itself. If you need a new Artix-7 FPGA side-channel target today, NewAE's current lineup points two different directions instead: the smaller CW312T-XC7A35 on their newer modular CW312/CW313 target system for something closer to the CW305's own scope, or the much larger CW310 'Bergen Board' ($5,310, Kintex-7 K410T) if you actually need SoC/OpenTitan-scale emulation. Neither is a drop-in replacement for the CW305's specific form factor and price point, so treat 'buy a CW310 instead' with caution - it may be the wrong tier entirely for what the CW305 was doing.

name: GlitchCaster
firmware_note: GlitchCaster ships with no onboard MCU and no firmware of its own - it is a PWM-driven high-voltage flyback circuit that needs an external GPIO/PWM controller to actually fire. An optional bundle adds a simple Raspberry Pi Pico controller board, which would run PicoEMP-compatible firmware, but that is a separate add-on, not part of the base unit.
price_note: The Crowd Supply page is still 'Coming Soon' as of 2026-09-10 with 0 updates posted and no funding campaign launched - there is no price to check yet, only a sign-up-for-updates form.
skill_note: It ships with no built-in controller - you must supply and program your own PWM/GPIO source to actually time and fire pulses, on top of the usual EMFI skill (finding a fault-sensitive spot and timing window on a live target) and the safety knowledge to handle a device that stores hundreds of volts.
build_note: No soldering described: a resin-shielded high-voltage PCB, a miniature coil-adapter board (leaded or SMA), a pre-made 4.7uH probe coil, and 24-inch jumper wires to your own controller. An optional bundle adds a simple Pi Pico controller board for people who want to start firing pulses immediately.
summary: An open-hardware EMFI (electromagnetic fault injection) probe head from a small Colorado-based team (Diffused Tactics), explicitly built on Colin O'Flynn's open-source PicoEMP design - the same design behind NewAE's own ChipSHOUTER-PicoEMP kit already in this database. It generates a roughly 250V pulse through a leaded or SMA probe coil via an LDA111/ATB3225-based flyback circuit and a 630V/470nF storage capacitor, but unlike PicoEMP it deliberately ships with no built-in controller - instead it uses 40mm-fan mounting so it can be bolted to a 3D printer or CNC head for repeatable XYZ-staged glitch mapping, with a coil adapter that accepts either leaded or SMA probe coils interchangeably.
honest_take: Do not confuse 'inspired by PicoEMP' with 'better than PicoEMP' - GlitchCaster is explicitly the same ~250V flyback circuit, and PicoEMP is open-source CC-BY-SA hardware you can build yourself or buy pre-built as NewAE's own ChipSHOUTER-PicoEMP Kit for $100. What GlitchCaster is actually selling is not more voltage or a new attack capability, it is mechanical: 40mm-fan mounting so you can bolt it to a 3D printer or CNC gantry for repeatable XYZ probe positioning, plus a coil adapter that takes both leaded and SMA coils, neither of which the stock PicoEMP kit provides out of the box. Whether that mechanical convenience is worth paying for over a $100 PicoEMP kit plus your own 3D-printed mount depends entirely on the eventual price, which does not exist yet - as of this check the project has never launched a Crowd Supply campaign, has zero updates, and its promised open-source GitHub repo does not exist publicly yet either, so right now there is nothing to buy and nothing independently verifiable beyond the campaign page's own claims. Treat every capability claim here as vendor-stated until backers actually receive hardware.

People who want to swap between leaded and SMA probe coils without rebuilding a rig

name: ChipJabber Unplugged
firmware: n/a (discrete analog/TTL logic, no MCU on the glitcher itself)
firmware_note: The glitcher itself is built from discrete components (comparators/timers and manual potentiometers) with 'not a single piece of programmable logic anywhere in sight,' by design - that is the whole teaching point. The bundled NOTDuino demo target is a real Arduino-programmable MCU board, separate from the glitcher.
price_note: Never launched. The Crowd Supply page still reads 'This project is launching soon... Coming Soon' with 0 updates - the GitHub repo's last commit is 16 September 2020 and Circuit Cellar covered the design in July 2020, so this has sat unlaunched for six years with no price ever posted.
skill_note: NewAE pitches it explicitly as 'designed more for fun than real-life usage' and as a hands-on way to learn what voltage fault injection actually is - you turn physical potentiometers and watch a boot process fail or succeed, no software required for the glitcher itself. The included NOTDuino target does need basic Arduino IDE familiarity to reprogram.
build_note: Three variants: the base Kit is through-hole parts buildable on a breadboard/perfboard from the schematic; the Mini is a pre-built SMD unit (not sold as a kit) powered by 3xAA batteries with large slider potentiometers; the Old-School PCB variant is a simplified double-sided design meant for home-etching or a PCB mill (sized to fit the Bantam PCB Mill's work area).
summary: A deliberately simple, no-programmable-logic voltage fault-injection tool from NewAE (the ChipWhisperer/ChipSHOUTER company) meant to teach the mechanics of glitching by hand: it drops a target's core voltage momentarily at a manually-timed instant during boot, using discrete analog circuitry and physical potentiometers instead of software. It pairs with NewAE's 'NOTDuino' demo board, which uses an EEPROM as a naive boot-time 'key' check, so you can watch the glitch actually defeat it. NewAE's own pitch is explicit that for real work you want ChipWhisperer or ChipSHOUTER instead - this exists to teach the concept, not to do the job professionally.
honest_take: Judge this by what it actually is, not what it might become: it has read 'Coming Soon' on Crowd Supply since before 2020, the GitHub repo's last commit is from September 2020, and NewAE's own page still says 'this project is launching soon' with zero updates posted in six years. That is not a slow-burn crowdfunding campaign, that is an abandoned commercial launch for a design that otherwise works fine - the open schematics and NOTDuino demo are real and documented, and NewAE's own campaign page tells you plainly to buy ChipWhisperer or ChipSHOUTER-PicoEMP instead once you outgrow it. If you want to actually own one, your only route right now is building it yourself from the public GitHub schematics - there was never a functioning 'buy it' path, so DIY was effectively always the only real option despite being marketed as three purchasable variants.

name: EPIC Erebus
firmware_note: Ships intended to run a default open-source ECP5 bitstream for standalone memory acquisition and patch/match, but the entire pitch is that gateware, firmware and toolchain are open so you build/modify your own rather than run one fixed vendor image. As of the check date the linked GitHub org (github.com/epic-erebus) is a placeholder with no published source.
price_note: No price has been set. The Crowd Supply campaign page is marked 'Coming Soon' with 0 updates and 0 backers; only an email signup for launch notification exists.
skill_note: Pitched explicitly around protocol-layer tinkering (open PCIe implementation, deep gateware modification), a level beyond just running pre-built PCILeech firmware on a Squirrel-class board.
build_note: Intended to sell as a finished M.2 2230 card, no soldering. Installing it means opening the target machine and fitting it into a free M.2 slot (or an adapter), which is inherently physical-access work.
summary: A pre-launch M.2 2230 FPGA card built around a Lattice ECP5 (ECP5-25 or ECP5-5G-85) for PCIe-based direct memory access research, positioned as PCILeech-compatible. Unlike bench-style PCIe DMA cards, it's sized and marketed to live permanently inside a laptop's internal M.2 slot and run standalone - acquiring memory and doing patch/match operations without a tethered host. Gateware, firmware and toolchain are promised fully open source. As of September 2026 it exists only as a pre-launch Crowd Supply listing with no price, no funded campaign, and no published source code.
honest_take: This is not a product you can buy yet: as of September 2026 the Crowd Supply page says 'launching soon,' with zero backers, zero updates, no price, and a linked GitHub org (github.com/epic-erebus) that contains nothing. Compared to the already-shipping Screamer PCIe Squirrel - an Artix-7 card you plug into a desktop PCIe x1 slot when you want to run an attack, priced around EUR 159 - Erebus targets the opposite use case: an M.2 2230 card small enough to install inside a laptop's Wi-Fi/NVMe slot and leave there, which the vendor states outright ('you can keep installed inside your laptop'). That makes it a plausible internal implant rather than a bench tool, and shifts the threat model from 'plug a card in' to 'install something permanently and close the case.' The people behind it (Joe FitzPatrick of SecuringHardware.com and Piotr Esden-Tempski) have a genuine track record in hardware-security training and open FPGA tooling, so this reads as a credible upcoming project rather than vaporware in the pejorative sense - but today it is unpriced, unreleased, and the 'fully open gateware' claim can't be checked against any published source.

summary: A purpose-built ESP32-WROOM-32UE add-on board for the Flipper Zero, combining a battery-backed GPS module and a high-gain 2.4GHz antenna with a BPM Circuits fork of the ESP32 Marauder firmware. Unlike the Texas Flipper Boards competitor, its firmware target ships with Bluetooth/BLE compiled in, so it adds BLE scanning and spam on top of Wi-Fi wardriving. It writes wardriving data directly to the Flipper Zero's own microSD card and reports status via an onboard RGB NeoPixel and TX/RX LEDs.
honest_take: Strip the branding away and this is an ESP32-WROOM-32UE running a forked build of the same open-source Marauder firmware every ESP32 wardriving board runs - the real differentiators are a battery-backed GPS module (faster first satellite fix than a bare GPS chip) and a purpose-built PCB with Bluetooth left switched on, unlike the $120 Texas Flipper Boards competitor, whose stock firmware target has Bluetooth explicitly compiled out. At $100 this is $20 cheaper and, on that evidence, the more capable of the two boards. The catch: the fork's own configs.h reports firmware version v1.2.1 while the upstream project it's based on is at v1.16.0, meaning it's frozen well behind current Marauder - newer scan/detection modes (Flock Safety camera detection, newer BLE spam variants, and other features added to upstream since) may simply not be present here, and there's no way to tell without the vendor publishing a changelog. It has no storage of its own - everything is written to the Flipper's SD card - and the original dual-core ESP32 (not an S2/S3/C-series part) means 2.4GHz-only Wi-Fi with no 5GHz visibility. As of September 2026 BPM Circuits has stopped taking orders, so neither board in this comparison is actually purchasable right now.

name: Pwnagotchi Hat (UPS/GPS/AC WiFi/USB Hub/RTC)
firmware_note: Bare expansion board with no firmware of its own. It exists to carry hardware for the Pwnagotchi project (already a separate tracked entry) — you flash Pwnagotchi's own OS image onto a microSD card yourself.
price_note: Vendor lists $74.50; currently sold out with a waitlist and a 3-5 business day ship estimate once restocked. Does not include a Raspberry Pi Zero/Zero W/Zero 2 W, microSD card, or 18650 cell — all sold separately.
skill_note: You still need to source a Pi Zero, flash a Pwnagotchi image yourself, and configure it — the hat has no setup wizard or onboarding of its own.
build_note: Solderless: mounts on the Pi Zero's GPIO header. You supply the Pi Zero (W or 2 W), a microSD card, and flash Pwnagotchi's own image — the board ships with no software pre-loaded. An optional backplate holds a user-supplied 18650 cell for up to ~4 hours runtime per the vendor.
summary: A Raspberry Pi Zero expansion board that bundles the specific hardware Pwnagotchi needs to run standalone: a dual-band MediaTek MT7612U USB WiFi chipset (the vendor states it is the same chipset as Alfa's AWUS036ACM, independently confirmed via a third-party listing), a USB-serial GPS module with PPS output, a UPS circuit for an optional 18650 cell, an internal 4-port USB hub, and a battery-backed RTC. It is bare hardware only — you provide the Pi Zero and flash Pwnagotchi's own OS image yourself.
honest_take: This is an integration convenience, not new capability: every function on this hat exists separately for less (an MT7612U dongle, a USB GPS puck, an RTC module, a USB hub), and Pwnagotchi itself is free, open-source software that has never shipped pre-installed on any commercial product, per its own install docs. What the ~$75 buys is not having to wire four separate peripherals into a Pi Zero's single USB port and GPIO header, plus a UPS so the unit survives being carried around. It ships as a bare board — no Pwnagotchi pre-installed, no Pi included, no SD card slot of its own (it rides on the Pi's) — budget extra money and 30-60 minutes of flashing and config before it does anything, and don't mistake 'purpose-built for Pwnagotchi' on the product page for 'comes with Pwnagotchi.'

name: ALFA AWUS036ACHM
firmware_note: Pure hardware NIC. Monitor mode and injection come from the host OS's in-kernel mt76 driver family plus whatever software you run (aircrack-ng, Wireshark, Kismet) — there is no vendor firmware relevant to security features.
price_note: lab401 (the reseller named in the brief) lists it at €59.00, ≈$63.72 at the FX rate checked. That's a real premium: the identical hardware sells for $36-49 at general electronics resellers (Getic ~$43, Rokland $48.97). lab401 also showed a $79 figure in a separate cached listing that could not be reconciled with the live €59 page — flagged as unresolved rather than picking one arbitrarily.
skill_note: Plug-and-play driver-wise on modern Linux (mt76 is in-tree, no DKMS) — Rokland's own driver guide calls MediaTek chipsets 'plug and play' — but getting real use out of monitor mode/injection means comfort with aircrack-ng/Wireshark/Kismet.
build_note: Buy and plug into USB. No assembly or flashing of the adapter itself; you configure whatever OS runs on the attached computer.
summary: Alfa's 'Mini' dual-band adapter: a MediaTek MT7610U chipset, AC600 class (150 Mbps 2.4GHz / 433 Mbps 5GHz), two RP-SMA connectors for external dipole antennas, and a screen-clip mount, aimed at laptop users who want monitor mode and packet injection with in-kernel Linux support. It is easily confused with the larger, older, RTL8812AU-based AWUS036ACH — despite the near-identical name, they use different chipsets, different USB connectors (Mini-USB here vs USB-C on the ACH) and different AC classes (AC600 vs AC1200).
honest_take: This is 'just a Wi-Fi adapter' in the most literal sense: no display, no attack software, nothing beyond an MT7610U chip and two antenna jacks — and notably no Bluetooth radio at all, unlike the newer AXM adapter in this same product line. Everything useful it does — monitor mode, deauth, handshake capture — comes from free software (aircrack-ng, Wireshark, Kismet) running on your laptop. The chipset itself is fine: MT7610U has mature in-kernel mt76 driver support with no DKMS wrestling, independently confirmed by community documentation (morrownr's USB-WiFi project). But it's a lower tier than the name suggests — AC600, not the AC1200 that at least one reseller's own product title confusingly implies — and it is a cheaper, different chipset from the RTL8812AU in the plain (non-M) 'AWUS036ACH.' Categorized here as 'wifi' rather than 'accessory' because monitor-mode/injection support is a deliberate, marketed feature this chipset was selected for. Be clear-eyed that you're paying for a driver-compatible commodity chip, not proprietary capability — lab401's price is a real premium over general electronics resellers for identical hardware.

summary: An open-source, dual-ESP32-WROOM-32U wardriving rig: one ESP32 handles WiFi scanning, the other handles Bluetooth/BLE scanning plus peripherals (ATGM336H GPS, optional SIM800L cellular module, SSD1306 OLED status display, DS18B20 temperature sensor). Everything logs to a microSD card as WiGLE-format CSV, with the current firmware able to upload directly to WiGLE.net. Joseph Hewitt publishes schematics, Gerbers and firmware on GitHub under GPL-3.0; the bare PCB is normally sold via Tindie, with DIY kits and assembled units available from independent third-party resellers.
honest_take: Confirmed as a genuinely distinct project from the 'C5 Wardriver' already in this database, not the same thing under a different name: this rig splits WiFi and Bluetooth scanning across two separate, older ESP32-WROOM-32U modules (2.4GHz-only silicon) rather than one newer single-chip solution, a deliberate architectural choice, not an oversight. It requires real through-hole soldering unless you pay a third-party reseller extra for a pre-built unit — the original creator's own bare-PCB Tindie listing is currently paused and won't ship to the US, so US buyers are pushed toward third-party kits by default. The firmware is unusually healthy for a single-maintainer hobby project: 368 GitHub stars, 40 forks, and commits into 2026 (OTA updates, direct WiGLE upload, a NimBLE migration for Bluetooth). But this is not a flash-only device — budget real assembly time and a soldering iron, or pay significantly more for someone else's assembled unit.

summary: A compact WiFi 6E adapter built around a MediaTek MT7921AUN combo chip (no separate general-purpose MCU) covering 2.4/5/6GHz WiFi plus Bluetooth 5.2, with two RP-SMA connectors for detachable dipole antennas and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A connector. Sold into the pentest/wardriving market specifically for its Linux monitor-mode and injection support, which is real but newer and less mature than Alfa's older Realtek-based adapters.
honest_take: The MT7921AUN's monitor-mode and injection support on Linux is genuinely usable today — in-kernel mt7921u driver, no DKMS needed on kernel 5.18+ — but it is not the drop-in-and-forget experience of an older RTL8812AU adapter. Community reports (morrownr's USB-WiFi reference doc, and two open GitHub issues filed against this exact chipset/driver combination — one against morrownr/USB-WiFi, one against openwrt/mt76) describe passive monitor mode working well while 'active monitor mode' has a documented history of breaking the driver, only recently reported fixed on kernel 6.12 and later. If your workflow needs rock-solid injection today, the Realtek-based AWUS036ACH/ACHM are a safer bet; if you specifically need 6GHz/WiFi 6E visibility or onboard Bluetooth 5.2 (which the ACHM lacks entirely), there is no Realtek alternative and this is the adapter for it. As with the other Alfa adapter in this batch, it's 'just' a combo WiFi/BT chip in a plastic shell with two antenna jacks — the actual attack tooling is separate free software you run on your computer, not anything on the device. No GPS either, despite marketing copy about 'portable WiFi analysis' that could be mistaken for a wardriving feature.
